utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are sorry for the delay, because of a possible fire alarm, but now we have been told it's quite okay. Before we start, there is a time schedule announcement. Next Monday and Tuesday, we will sit in the afternoon session. From Wednesday, we will sit in the morning session for two weeks. Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, one procedural matter and again, in the interests of not disclosing potential protected witnesses could we go to private session for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, you may proceed. Examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can look at me.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I can see you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to give you some instructions, like I do to all the witnesses. Let me just tell you that you have a screen, a computer in front of you, and can you see the moving dot?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please pay attention to the dot. When the dot stops, start giving your answer both to me and to my learned friend, the Prosecutor. We both speak the same language, and the most important thing is that my question and your answer do not overlap, and what is very important is that your answers are interpreted correctly and our interpreters have to have the time to do that because everything you say is interpreted in two languages in English and French. If you speak too fast, your answer will be lost in translation.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your cooperation. My first question to you is can you first tell us your name, your first name, your last name, where were you born, your short CV up to 1990?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you for the opportunity that you have given me to talk about the time and the events. My name is Ivan Bagaric I was born in 1962 in Tomislavgrad municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is where I completed my elementary and secondary education. After that, I enrolled at the school of medicine in Sarajevo, from which I graduated in 1986. After that, I worked as a MD in Tomislavgrad in the medical centre. So that was up to 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you please tell us what were your duties, the duties that you discharged after 1990?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: After 1990, I continued working as an MD --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please slow down, look at the dot.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: So I continued working as an MD, as a general practitioner, in the first free election in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as a doctor, I was elected as a member of parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was in 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you say as a doctor? Were you a member of a party?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: What I wanted to say was that I was a member of the Croatian democratic union, but I continued working as a general practitioner in the medical centre until 1992. In 1992, I joined the main medical corps, i.e., one of the components of the Croatian Defence Council, which was on the strength of the Croatian Defence Council. Obviously, at the time, I was also a member of the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1993, what duties did you discharge?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: In 1993 I was the commander of the main medical staff of the Croatian Defence Council, and that was the period during which the parliament stopped holding sessions because of the war events in Bosnia and Herzegovina and around it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will come to that later. I just wanted you to inform the Chamber of the duties that you discharged. So throughout 1993, you were the commander of the medical staff?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992, entire 1993, and entire 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discharge any other duties in 1993 and in 1994?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's try and clarify that. Only yesterday, we heard in this courtroom that you were the Health Minister of the Croatian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I hear this for the first time. No, I never was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday it was alleged here in the courtroom that this was published by the Croatian Radio?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: When? Nowadays?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No in 1993 it was published it was said on the Radio that you were the Minister of Health of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I told you exactly what my position was during 1993. So do I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I understand that you were never the Minister of Health of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's start with my first questions. We have still not had a witness here who was a member of the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So could you tell us in simple words about the work of the parliament at that time in 1993? Who were the deputies, what decisions were made, and when did it stop existing?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: The parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina consisted of two chambers. The Chamber of peoples -- I apologise. I made a mistake. So the Chamber of citizens and the Chamber of municipalities. I was a member of the Chamber of municipalities and I was there on behalf of Tomislavgrad municipality. The parliament was made up of three political parties, which accounted for a large majority in the parliament. These political parties were ethnically based. The Croatian Democratic Union, the Serbian Democratic Party and the Party of Democratic Action. I believe that there were some other, little parties with just a few seats in the parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can speed up a little. I can see that you're following the transcript but you can still speed up a little.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: It is very interesting to note how these parties thought at the time, i.e., what were the goals they fought for. The Croatian Democratic Union wanted a sovereign and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Party of Democratic Action also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I didn't want to be on my feet too soon because I thought perhaps this would be just a passing topic. However, on behalf of the Prosecution, I object to this testimony, and any further testimony about the parliament or about political matters. The only notice given by this witness under Rule 65 ter as required by the Rules is that this witness would talk about medical matters, he was a chief of medical headquarters, medical attention given at the war hospital. It is entirely relates to the providing of medical care in the city of Mostar. There was absolutely no notice given that this would be a political witness, we are hearing this now for the first time. Of course we don't have any prior statements because we never get prior statements so we object to this testimony at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you promised us that you will get over this section as soon as possible, as part of the background of this witness. Let's come to the subject matter of the testimony of this witness as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. I already announced that. I just wanted to lay a certain background because the gentleman had a certain duty and I thought it would be important for this Chamber to hear about the workings of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina because that was the first and the last parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the gentleman was a deputy in the parliament and he has his own personal knowledge and this is the only thing that he was going to tell us about. And I have only one question about that and I thought this would be very interesting and your learned -- my learned friend, this was not too soon. I expected you to react even sooner than you actually did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you heard the objection of my learned friend. I announced you as a witness who would be talking on a different matter but you have personal knowledge of the workings of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You were a deputy. Can you tell us in very, very short outlines, about the main events in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time? Or maybe I could lead you. Maybe that would be better. Please, can you tell us whether you were in coalition, whether HDZ was in coalition with the SDA in the parliament? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that the events that took place in the Bosnia and Herzegovina immediately, on the eve of the war, were very interesting and I would like to ask you to study the transcripts and what the parliament looked like, so the HDZ and SDA were two parties that were fighting for the independence of Bosnia. This is corroborated by the fact that we first voted for the declaration on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in order to adopt that declaration, we needed a two third majority of the votes in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina. All HDZ and SDA deputies voted in favour of that declaration. This was the first precondition for the referendum on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. When the decision was made on the referendum, all Serbian deputies headed by their leaders, left the parliament and started the war. All I wanted to say was that as a deputy in the parliament, as a doctor, I contributed towards the creation of Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I renew our objection. Mr. Krsnik said he had one question. This is now going on it's clearly entitled going on to political matters which this Chamber has heard weeks and weeks of testimony about. In addition to being unannounced and unnoticed it is also completely cumulative. I think the Chamber has heard from many witnesses about the referendum in the early 1992 and as far as I know it's not even a disputed matter. A majority of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina of Croats and Muslims voted for an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is unnoticed evidence and it is cumulative. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, shall we come to the subject matter of the testimony of this witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, certainly. I will move to the subject matter, but I always believed that there is -- when it comes to the time of which we were listening for six months in the Prosecution's presentation of witnesses, it is never too much to hear about these times and the gentleman here participated in the political life of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time in the events that determined the subsequent destiny of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, I'll move on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to another subject, and tell us, during the war, or on the eve of the war, what were your duties, where were you, what did you do at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: As a doctor, I realised that the war was inevitable, after the beginning of conflicts, i.e., Serbian attacks on Croatian areas, that is on Croatian villages, I started to organise the health protection of the population, together with my colleagues on the ground. We established the main medical corps, which -- the main medical headquarters which was one of the first organised units of the Croatian Defence Council, which defended the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Since the structure of my headquarters is not the subject matter of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is, actually?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, I no longer know what the subject matter is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, please, could you follow my questions? Would you be so kind and tell us about the establishment of the headquarters and what your role was in that? How was it established and how did it function during the war, at the beginning of the war, who were its members?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: On the eve of the open conflict and during the conflict started by the Serbs, we established the main medical headquarters in order to protect primarily our civilians but also our soldiers. We did that because the system of health protection at the beginning of 1992 in Bosnia and Herzegovina, was practically non-existent. When ties with Sarajevo were severed, when the central government was blocked, we who were then on the ground, had to respond to that situation and protect the people. We made rounds of those areas for which we considered that they would find themselves in the immediate threat of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption. Would it help you if you saw the exhibit D1/375? Can we put D1/375 on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: After the inspection of the area, we decided where we would -- we were going to put up our medical points. At the beginning, they were usually in the medical centres, which later on were transformed into war hospitals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you can turn towards the exhibit. You have a pointer or you will be given a pointer. So can you tell us about the organisation on the ground, municipal, county -- municipalities, counties?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: On parallel with the work that we were doing at the time, we made rounds of the ground and we appointed municipal medical chiefs because the whole organisation was based at the municipal level. People were defending their own municipalities, their own villages, and they didn't move anywhere, at the time they stayed put and they defended their own homes. So all of our hospitals, I believe that there were 13 of them, were established during 1992. That is at the beginning of 1992, before and during the conflicts with the Serbs, i.e., during the aggression on the part of the Serbs. So in Tomislavgrad, the war hospital was established in 1992, or in Livno also, in Mostar as well, in Grude. It is very interesting to see where all these institutions were. Some of them were in hotels, some of them were in medical centres, we even used even churches, hotels. I can see here that one of them was in a hospital, in a factory, in schools. So in all those places, that we deemed to be secure and protected. They were referred to as war hospitals but they looked after everybody alike, civilians and soldiers, primarily because of the fact that some parts of our areas were completely cut off from the previously existing larger institutions and bigger hospitals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, would you please be kind enough to tell us what is the source of this document? As you asked in the past many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who is the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: This is my document. So the source of this document is my master's thesis, the subject of which is the organisation of health protection during the war, and this thesis has been published because it served as the background for a paper that I have also published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to tell us whether you created these medical centres together with Muslims, with Bosniaks? Did you cooperate and did that relationship change over time? Did it or did it not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your question. Your Honours, I would like to tell you that whatever we did at the time, we did together with our Muslim colleagues, doctors, and not only with them, with everybody else. In our hospitals, we had Serbian, Croatian and Muslim employees. Also during all of the conflicts, we stayed together and we treated everybody across the board. The first problem arose with the beginning of conflict between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council. So the army that defended Bosnia but which clashed eventually. It was then when we lost some of these hospitals. For example, the hospital in Bugojno which we equipped, we prepared, but when Bugojno was taken by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and when the Croatian population was expelled from that municipality, we obviously lost the hospital. The same happened in Jablanica. So the hospital in Jablanica was the hospital which was an off-shoot of the Mostar war hospital, and there we treated everybody during the conflict with the Serbs. However, after the -- with the development of the situation in the Neretva valley, we lost that hospital as well, and in some of the areas across Bosnia-Herzegovina, such as Tuzla, Bosanska Bijela, so Bosanska, Posavina, Tolisa, the northern parts of Bosnia, all the time we worked together until the end of the war and this cooperation was never interrupted or discontinued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you briefly tell the Trial Chamber what the principles were on which the medical headquarters based itself?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: The working principles in our institutions were as follows, were the following. First of all, we worked in an integrated manner, that is to say we took care of everyone, we treated everyone. Women, children, soldiers and civilians, old people, young people. Thousands of babies were born in our hospitals. So perhaps it's not good to say -- it's not good to call those hospitals war hospitals because in the medical profession, a war profession refers to something entirely different. However, we called them war hospitals because they were located in war surroundings and secondly, the second principle which we respected in those hospitals was that everyone should be treated equally. I would like to inform this venerable court that our hospitals treated all patients, regardless of their nationality, regardless of whether a son was treated as a member of this army or that army, or regardless of the fact that someone had perhaps even committed a crime. He would be treated and in exactly the same way, and with exactly the same level of competence. And as I have already said, I'm afraid that the Prosecutor might object to me repeating this, I would like to repeat that in our institutions, all doctors, regardless of their nationality worked together. No one was ever dismissed from those institutions because he was a member of another nationality. And no one was ever rejected throughout those war years without being offered help because he was a member of another nationality or a member of some other army. I can claim this as a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your medical headquarters organised on a volunteer basis or was mobilisation involved or something else?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I'm glad that you have put this question to me because I would like to say how our organisation was an exclusively voluntary organisation. It's true to say that during the war, I did write orders because I didn't know how else to address people in the course of the war. I didn't write requests for something to be done but I never wrote an order according to which someone had to work in a hospital or according to which someone had to go here or there, except if that meant offering help, except in cases when help had to be offered or when someone's life had to be saved or if it meant perhaps in areas where there were no doctors but many civilians and soldiers had been wounded or suffered, when they needed help, we would do so, I would write orders for this. So our organisation worked on an exclusively voluntary basis and no one was forced to do anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you be so kind as to tell us whether you had any experience of organisations, headquarters, medical headquarters in those extraordinary circumstances, had you had any experience prior to these events or did you gain this experience in the course of the events?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: As a representative in parliament I observed what was happening in Croatia. So the aggression against Croatia, by the Serbian paramilitary units and the Yugoslav army. I took this to be an aggression against human rights and against freedom. And I was interested to see what my colleagues, other doctors in Croatia were doing. Similarly, as up until then we had been living in the same state, in Yugoslavia, we had cooperation with Croatian doctors, with Croatian hospitals, from earlier on, and I personally went to Zagreb at the beginning of the war and I visited the main medical headquarters in Croatia which, at the beginning, initially, was organised as a civilian institution, and later on, Mr. Prodan, Commander Prodan, became its head. I told him, "As a doctor, if it's necessary, I'm at your disposal." Because the casualties in Croatia -- this was taking place very near my house. There is no more than three kilometres, a few kilometres from my house to the border as the crow flies. We partially learned from them and partially to an extent I spent sometime in the hospital in Split. This hospital was about 80 kilometres away from Tomislavgrad or maybe 90 kilometres away from Tomislavgrad. Why was I there? First of all, I wanted to learn more about the organisation of health care in extraordinary circumstances. And secondly, many Croats from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and especially from Tomislavgrad, at the beginning of the war in Croatia, they went to defend Vukovar, Dubrovnik, Zadar, Sibenik and Split on a voluntary basis and I was worried about their fate. They were my neighbours. So this is what I had experienced. And of course, this was not sufficient. But it was important for me. If I was going to develop a system which was quite different from a civilian one. And now I think that I am a lot more capable for such organisations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, I believe this Chamber is only interested in the incidents that happened in 1993, that is during the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats during that period. Please concentrate your testimony on that period.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mentioned Split, the hospital in Split, can you tell us what role it had in the course of 1993? Do you personally know how many wounded there were, how many people were treated? Did you personally cooperate with that hospital in the course of 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Sometimes I go off on a tangent, it's true, but Your Honours believe me this is my first time I've been here and I'm slightly nervous. So in 1993, the hospital in Split, in the course of that year, and before that year as well as later on, the hospital in Split was a hospital to which we would send all those who had been seriously wounded. We didn't have any medical centres. We didn't have the possibility of providing quality health care. And this is why we sent many patients to the hospital in Split. Tens of thousands, I would say. I know as a fact that all those from Bosnia and Herzegovina were patients in the hospital in Split. I think that there were at least about 15.000 Croats there. And I think almost 4.000 Muslims, either civilians or soldiers. In the course of that entire period, the hospital in Split was open to us. It was open to us and to the Muslims and during the conflict with the Muslims. That never ceased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of 1993 and 1994, throughout that period?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, throughout 1992, 1993 and 1994. Right up until the end of the war, when Sarajevo, the blockade of Sarajevo was raised as well as the blockade of Tuzla which were medical centres, where there were medical centres and which could then take over the role of the institutions which were taking care of those who had been most seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have enough personnel? Did you have enough medical supplies and equipment? Could you briefly tell us about this, to see what the situation was in the course of 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: There was a shortage of everything. We didn't have enough doctors. Especially specialists. Surgeons, who were indispensable, in order to establish such a system, such a health system in wartime situation. Similarly, we didn't have enough equipment, we didn't have sufficient medical supplies. And all these problems were the result of the fact that three big medical centres in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Banja Luka, Tuzla, and Sarajevo, and several regional centres, such as Zenica, Travnik, they were outside of the other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These parts were totally closed and blocked off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me as a follow-up to this question, if we could concentrate on Mostar or the surroundings, the areas that you are personally familiar with in Bosnia-Herzegovina, how were the Muslims, the Bosniaks, organised? And I'm referring primarily to your colleagues, to other doctors.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the Trial Chamber will most -- will be interested in this segment most of all, in the course of 1993, which relates to the organisation of health care in Mostar, that is to say the organisation of health in the hospital in Mostar, which at the time was a wartime hospital, a war hospital in Mostar. First of all, I would like to point something out --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if I can lead you, would you be so kind, Mostar is a special subject but could you tell us how your colleagues, your other doctors, Muslims, Bosniaks, how they organised, just as a sort of introduction, just in general terms? I can't put suggestive questions to you. My questions have been very general so please could all your answers be very open but we just have to pay attention to the subject. Perhaps I could show you a document. You will tell the Trial Chamber what the source is. The document would be D1/376. Could you tell us what the cooperation was between you? Was it organised independently or together? You know what I mean.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: May I start or should I wait?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait to have a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have managed to translate everything and all the documents are in English.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document that I signed. And which refers to the 27th of September, to that period, so it was at the end or in the second half of 1992. This is proof that we doctors started developing a health system together in those parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina which were not under occupation, which had not been occupied by the Serbs. So, for example, here in the order they mention that it is necessary to exchange the personnel, the team, in the Jablanica war hospital. At the time, Croats and Muslims were being treated in that hospital, although the Muslims are in the majority in Jablanica. And although most of the personnel in Jablanica were Muslims. And I issued this order so that the surgical team from the war hospital in Mostar should go and replace the surgical team in Jablanica because there was no surgery ward in that hospital before the war. So the hospital in Jablanica was a sort of branch of the war hospital in Mostar. And then in the second paragraph of this order, there is the second claim. I say immediately send surgical team to Travnik, so it means that at the time of the defence of Travnik, which was defended by Muslims and the Croats together, under the leadership of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, it means that in that hospital, there was not a sufficient number of doctors there or rather it means that the doctors had no relief, they didn't have the opportunity of having a rest so it was important to reassign those doctors. It was important to help them. And this is proof, this is something that can prove that we cooperated. Muslim doctors, colleagues, joined our organisation. We worked together. As I have already said, that cooperation continued, mostly, right up to the end of the war and it never ceased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours I would just like an instruction from you. This was always the time for a break. Are we going to adhere to that schedule or are we going to continue because it's already half past three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It depends how long your direct examination will go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think because we got quite a lot of documents, that I want to go through, which I want to introduce through this witness, because he is the author, I think it's going to it take another hour or an hour and a half at least because of the number of documents that we have. It will be less than what I said in the summary. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I quite understand. But I hope you could finish your direct examination before next break. We will break now until 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to say that I am not sure that I will finish by the end of this break, because I think that the testimony of this witness could be of great help to this Trial Chamber because we have four major subjects, three of which refer to testimony given before this Trial Chamber. We'll try to see what this witness knows about that. Sovici and Doljani will be a special subject because this witness has personal knowledge about it. That's quite a major subject. And then the subject of Mostar and the Mostar war hospital as well as the detention centres, or the central military prison in the Heliodrom. We also have quite a lot of documents and this is the beginning of this background. Perhaps you consider that it is an introductory part and that we have heard a lot about this already but there is always something knew that you hear from witnesses who have particular information about these matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So doctor, let's turn to these more important so to speak matters and let's try to hear what you know with regard to the war hospital in Mostar, and let me put a question to you immediately. We've heard two witnesses in this -- before this Trial Chamber about that matter. According to the testimony of one of the witnesses, you carried a weapon in the hospital and it wasn't -- they didn't know who you were exactly. Could you please comment on this? As this was a witness who gave testimony, open testimony, this was Mr. Van der Grinten an observer of the European Union and he said that he became acquainted Mr. Bagaric, with a certain Mr. Bagaric. Was there another Mr. Bagaric in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he said that you were armed in the hospital. And that there wasn't much cooperation. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know whom I could ask about my rights. If this is correct, if someone made these claims, what rights do I have if none of this is correct? Can I, for example, institute proceedings against him or can I call him to provide an explanation about this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Just say what you have to say and the Trial Chamber shall bring a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- the Defence counsel put the case to you and you have the full right to dispute with this allegation in this courtroom. Whatever you said will be registered in the transcript. Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I considered objecting before and then the witness's response exactly confirmed that I should have in fact objected. Mr. President, I object to the manner of putting questions to the witnesses, identifying other witnesses in the case, even if they were p in public session. I believe it's sufficient for the counsel to put to the witness quite clearly the question, when you worked in the hospital, did you carry -- did you carry a firearm. There is no reason public or non-public to go into these long, argumentive statements about what some other witness said. I object to that, and if that then been done -- if that had been done, excuse me, we hopefully would not have had the personal outburst of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, witness, you may simply answer the question, whether you carried a weapon or not at that time, and then the Defence counsel will ask you the follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. So I can quite responsibly claim before all of you here that before you, you have a man who never carried a weapon, no kind of weapon, and no kind of pistol, throughout the entire period of war. And as far as I know, according to the Geneva Convention medical personnel can carry weapons if they go out into the field, et cetera. So it's -- there is nothing wrong if some did that but I, Ivan Bagaric, I personally never had a weapon, took a weapon in the course of the war, and no one ever saw me with a pistol hanging from my belt, and especially not in the hospital. That's quite incorrect. That's a lie. I was a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us for patients of Muslim nationality, do you know whether they were treated differently from members of other nationalities and were there cases where someone could come to the hospital and take them away where they wanted to take them to? We have heard testimony to this effect, not many, but we've heard testimony from one witness to this effect?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, I was the commander of the entire health system of the HVO in Posavina in central Bosnia and in Mostar. Each war hospital had its own commander, that is to say its own leadership and that is to say for the Mostar as well. Circumstances were such I spent that year, the year you're interested in, Your Honours, I spent that year in Mostar. So throughout the year 1993, I was in Mostar. And my office was located in one -- in a building which belonged to the war hospital, which was part of the war hospital complex. And I claim that a patient because he was a member of another peoples was never treated differently. How can I know that you might say that I didn't know each patient there so how do I know this? But I would like to convince you that all doctors who worked in the Mostar hospital, regardless of their nationality treated every one equally and I would certainly have found out if there had been cases in which people were treated differently. This never took place. And I understand the second part of your question and I will address it but I want to tell the Trial Chamber how we worked, because this is being recorded for history. This is important for me and for all of us. With regard to this second issue, this second question, we had a hospital in five locations in Mostar, in the town in which there was fighting, there was a war. So in a town -- well the buildings were surrounded by fighting, our surgery department was at the front line almost so we had to have security and we did security. We had military police, we had some kind of -- well, I can't say some kind of but we had people who were not sent to the battlefield and so on. Home guards, who were there and who guarded the entrance to the hospital. The hospital wasn't an institution anyone could go into. Whenever anyone entered the hospital he could be checked, registered, and there was one thing I would like to say now. To this very day, even in peace time, many hospitals have problems with relatives with patients who want to know more, who want someone to be treated in this way or in that way. And during the war, after someone had been killed or after someone had been wounded then his colleagues would enter and I think that doctors were even threatened if he's going to die I'm going to do this thing or that thing. But thank God, apart from such incidents, nothing else happened. If someone had been taken away from the hospital, a wounded person, because he was of a different nationality I would have known about that because if there was any kind of incident in the hospital or in the vicinity of the hospital I would have heard this from the commander of the hospital. I would have found out about it and I would have reacted. I can't remember a single incident a single case of someone taking someone away. So if such a thing had taken place, I would have known about it. And I never heard about such an incident. I categorically -- I would like to categorically state this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, according to your knowledge, were the patients allowed to sit around the hospital? I think that part is called Bijeli Brijeg in 1993, were they allowed to walk around the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I was not allowed to walk around the hospital because the situation was as it was, unfortunately. I don't know what you're aiming at but there were -- it was impossible for any of the patients walking around the hospital, if they were hospitalised, because I repeat, if somebody is hospitalised, then they are hospitalised. But during the war, when the shells are falling, when sniper fire is being opened, this is absolutely impossible. And I don't know of any hospital any patients roaming around freely around the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm again putting you this question because of some testimony that we've heard in this courtroom. Can you please tell us what was the longest time that a patient could spend in your hospital? Obviously I understand this depended on the diagnosis. But let's say a seriously wounded patient comes into your hospital, what would you do, what would you as the hospital in Mostar, how would you treat the patient?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was a GP and now I have a specialisation in public health. So I wasn't a surgeon then. I still am not a surgeon, and as regards the length of the treatment of certain patients, especially a surgical patient, the structure of injuries is different during the war than it is during the peace time. So there is a number of people who are injured who come to the hospital during the wartime. So surgeons were in charge of that and they decided how long somebody was going to spend in the hospital but the key issue here that a the Mostar hospital was not a safe hospital, which means that it was surrounded by fighting. It was in the war zone. And it was also not safe for the patients inside because the hospital was shelled and it was also not safe for the medical personnel. So we were forced, after the urgent treatment and triage --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please slow down? I'm listening to you and everything is being recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: So after the triage and the urgent treatment these patients were either discharged as fit to go home to or to their units or if their condition required a longer treatment and this was any treatment that extended a period of 15 to 20 days, these patients were then referred to Split, for so to say final treatment which included physiotherapy and other types of treatment. So our hospital was in the zone of war operations and we could not provide our patients with the full treatment. We could not keep them for as long as we would have wanted to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, in March, 1993, how would it have been possible for a patient from Sarajevo to come to Mostar for a hospital treatment? Can you please clarify? Do you personally know, let's say there is a patient in Sarajevo, it is March, 1993 and that same patient comes to Mostar for treatment. Did you ever have a case like that? Was that possible at all? What do you know about that, a case like that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Okay. March, 1993, is the time when Sarajevo was completely occupied. I apologise. It was isolated. It was under a blockade. It Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 12329 to 12336. was also the period when the communications with Mostar were interrupted. So there were no routes to Mostar which were free for passage. Whether anybody could have transferred with the help of UNPROFOR or some other organisation, I don't know, but it was not possible in a normal way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember any patient that stayed in the hospital from March, 1993, to July, 1993? So for four months.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I must say, and I have to be fully honest and say that I cannot -- I couldn't know every patient personally. We are talking about thousands of people here but it would be very unusual for anybody to stay in the hospital for such a long time, because by that time, they would either have been cured or referred for further treatment. So I don't know why would such a thing happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you well, the Mostar hospital was the hospital where only urgent care was provided, primary care was provided?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I have to correct you. It was not the hospital that provided primary care. If you say primary care, primary care is the care that is provided by general practitioners. The hospital in Mostar was an institution where we had neuropsychiatric patients, surgical patients, patients with internal diseases so it was at the level of the secondary care, health care, but at the time, during the war, unfortunately, we could not provide the full extent of that care because we did not have a neurosurgeon so we could not carry out any neurosurgical procedures. So that hospital was not the hospital that could provide the full extent of care to all the injured persons. People were either taken care of urgently and referred to another hospital or they were fully cured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's round up this subject and move on to Sovici and Doljani. I would like to show you D1/354. Can you tell the Honourable Court what this document means, who is its author and so on and so forth? While we are waiting for this document, can you tell us the approximate number in May, June, July, August, September, October, of 1993, how many patients did you treat? Who were Muslims or Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I was not concentrating. Can you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. Can you remember or give us an approximate figure from May, 1993 up to the end of 1993, how many Muslim patients did your hospital treat, cured or referred to other centres? And a subquestion: Did you, throughout 1993, have Muslim doctors working in the hospital? So two questions.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. We had as many Muslim patients as there were at the time. And I can't give you the exact figure but the number was rather large, several thousand, I would say. I cannot be very precise. I can talk about that but I cannot give you the -- a precise figure. There were many. I can't say that their number was equal as a number of Croats. There was probably a fewer number of them, but we never counted heads and we never counted who was who, and every patient regardless of their nationality or ethnic affiliation were treated the same. I would also like to say that no doctor, no member of staff, paramedic or any other member of staff, was dismissed, fired, because of their religion or national affiliation. I have an example that I would like to share with you, Your Honours. Throughout the entire war, the two key surgeons were two Serbs. Also, all the Muslims who stayed in Mostar remained working together with us, and all these people, after the war, were proposed to get ranks. Somebody asked me why should Dr. Ruzic be a colonel and my answer was that that person deserves all the respect and all the ranks that can be had. That was my attitude and that was the attitude of all of us across the board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please comment on this document, 354?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: This document, I remember. I remember why it was written.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the source?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: The source is the main medical headquarters of the HVO. I signed it -- this document personally, and among -- and this document served as the background material which I used in my master's thesis. This is a communication which was written, and issued, before the beginning of the first conflict. This was on the 14th of April, for fear of a possible conflict. So this document dates before the conflict with Muslims in Mostar. So this document is the result of our fears of the possible consequences in the city of Mostar, and as a result of a meeting that we had, we doctors had, in order to organise ourselves and decide what we were going to do, and the meeting was attended by Croats and Muslims, upon my -- on my initiative, I chaired the meeting, together with a commander, Dr. Kvesic and you can see from the text why was this meeting held, and why it resulted in a press release published on the Radio Mostar which was at that time controlled by the Muslim side and which brought some untruthful facts. These incorrect facts were relative to the things that were allegedly being done by Croats in Mostar. Unfortunately we were aware that these incorrect facts could have resulted in a separation between Muslim and Croat doctors, and that's why we wanted to support fighting, the joint fighting of Muslims and Croats against the common enemy. So this was the time unfortunately the time when there were already sporadic incidents between the Army of BH and the Croatian Defence Council. As a member of the Croatian Defence Council I was afraid that within the army, within one army that was defending the state against the aggression, I was afraid because that army was not under the unique command. It had two commanders. I was afraid that there would be conflicts. And that conflict, actually you could tell that there would be conflict even before this communication. Personally, without anybody's advice or about anybody's advice to the contrary, the end of 1992, I tried to establish some cooperation with the Muslim side. I tried to establish some cooperation with their chief of the medical staff, and I even offered him some solutions. I offered him the possibility to jointly sign some documents to work together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We understand that you're eager to give your testimony but Defence counsel asked you a very simple question. That is what is the source of this document. I think during the first few sentences, you have already answered that question. If the Defence counsel would like to ask more questions, he would, and you may answer his follow-up questions. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. There may have been a misunderstanding. I asked the witness to clarify the circumstances under which the document was drafted, and issued, and that is what I wanted the witness to tell us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are going to go back to the 9th of May and your relationship with Arif Pasalic and we are going to talk about all those whom you knew personally and had contacts with, but we are now going to move on to other documents. And I would like to ask you again general question, about the cooperation with the international organisations and whether you attended a meeting in Jablanica, whether you made rounds of Sovici and Doljani, and some other places on the 4th of May, 1993. What was the occasion of that visit? Who was a member of the delegation? Who was there? What was discussed there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I apologise, again, I've heard several questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I did not want to confuse you. Let's put you one question at a time. The first question is: Did you attend any meetings on 4th of May, 1993 in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, can somebody please move this paper? Because I can't see the transcript. Thank you very much. This meeting was held on my initiative. This may sound pretentious, because Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Halilovic, Mr. Morillon, and Mr. Morales attended that meeting. So yes, the answer is I did attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you speak too fast, what happens is that we end up with just two names instead of four. Can you please just slowly tell us where the meeting took place and who were the main participants in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: If the Honourable Court will allow me, I would first like to explain why I initiated that meeting, why I wanted that meeting to take place. We had learned that in some municipalities, to be more precise in some villages, in Kostajnica and in Neretvica, some crimes had been committed over the Croatian civilians, and those places were Buscak, Trusina. This all --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the name of the first village?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why we want you to repeat the name slowly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: The name is Buscak. Trusina. Seonica and so on and so forth. Again Seonica is spelled wrongly. Seonica. Again, it is not spelled correctly but let's not waste any more time. So this was on 14 April, and 16 April, so before any other conflicts. Unfortunately even before the open conflicts in central Bosnia or at the same time, in the second case it was at the same time and in the first case, it was before that. The members of the BH Army stormed into the villages which were not defended and they killed several civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour we would object to the relevance of this testimony. I thought there might be a medically related meeting in Jablanica. That's why I was just waiting to see where the testimony was going. This is simply once again tu quoque. Unless counsel can articulate a very specific other relevance for this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, just tell us about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, allow me to address the Chamber. I know that you are not familiar with this testimony and that all you know about it is what it says in the summary. I believe it is not -- it is not -- one should not be allowed to interrupt this meeting, who is going to talk -- tell us about the very crucial meeting in Jablanica. This has nothing to do with tu quoque. His thought -- that his train of thoughts was interrupted in midway. There were some objections on -- regarding the BH Army, with regard to the events in Sovici and Doljani and that is why the meeting took place. It is not correct it to interrupt the meeting midway in the middle of his sentence and all the objections, tu quoque objections, are raised every time when my learned friend finds something unsuitable, he gets up and with the objection tu quoque. And it is very relevant, very relevant because it is very important why the top army officials of the HVO and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina met, and then they went to visit Sovici and Doljani and then you will hear what happened later on. The Prosecutor had a videotape in this courtroom, showed us a videotape, and I will not allow my witness to be interrupted like this. I'm not allowed to say anything. I can't give you the testimony instead of the witness. I don't know how to do that so let's please allow my witness to explain everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, if your witness as a doctor had said in a number of small villages, there were Croat civilian victims, perhaps it wouldn't sound like tu quoque but to it use language like, members of the BH Army stormed into the villages, which were not defended and killed civilians, does sound a little bit like describing events in the war. Perhaps there is a different way to describe. He should be as a doctor I would imagine concerned about the death of civilians rather than the activities of an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I absolutely agree with you, Your Honour, Judge Clark, and I believe that this should be so. However, people are not used to giving testimony in this courtroom, and I believe that this witness has never been in any courtroom before. Your Honour, there were rumours circulating and people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour, once again counsel is giving testimony. There is no reason for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, let's allow my witness to give testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, witness, please come to that meeting in Jablanica directly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, allow me to tell you what I think and what I have to tell you, and not what I'm being suggested or instructed to tell you. Your Honour, Judge Clark, I did -- was not so much concerned about those who had been killed because I couldn't help them. I was concerned about the wounded because they require treatment and there was no way we could access to them. And it was my duty and my task to give them help. What else could I do but to be concerned, to ask questions, to beg around, who did I beg? Everybody, the Red Cross, the United Nations, everybody. I wrote several requests. Unfortunately, I had better information than other people. That's what my doctors told me. So on several occasions, I tried to go there in order to pull out those people who were wounded, in order to treat them. But since all my attempts failed, even with the help of the Red Cross, led by Mr. Mark Perot [phoen] who took us to Jablanica in ten ambulance cars, and then he was returned once and then he would return for a second time, and I -- unsuccessfully tried to get there. Then I asked Mr. Morales, who was the commander of the Spanish Battalion and I told him, "Mr. Morales, I believe it is also your task to enable me and my doctors to go there and help those people." And he agreed and I'm so grateful to him. So Morales invite Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Halilovic, to this meeting in Sovici after several failed attempts on my part to get to these places. And that is how this meeting took place, but rather late. Unfortunately. But as long as it happened. Better late than never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was that meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: That meeting was organised in the area under the control of UNPROFOR, the Spanish Battalion in Jablanica. So in their camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember all the participants in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Arif Pasalic at the meeting together with Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Sulejman Budakovic also known as Tetak?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately I spoke with Tetak before, but I cannot confirm that he was at the meeting but Halilovic and Pasalic were at the meeting. I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Rasim Delic present?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Honourable Court who these people were?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: The host of that meeting was Colonel Morales the commander of the Spanish Battalion in Medjugorje. There was Mr. Petkovic, the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO. There was me as the chief of the medical headquarters of the HVO. There was Mr. Halilovic, the commander of the BH Army. There was Mr. Pasalic, the commander of the Mostar zone of the BH Army and representatives of the red -- International Red Cross, I believe were at the meeting. So this is the answer to your question, who attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question now I would like to ask Madam Registrar to give you the document D1/367, Exhibit 1/368, Exhibit 1/379, D1/370, and 1/359. And finally, D1/381. When you get all these documents, could you examine them individually. The usher will put the English original on the ELMO and could you briefly tell us what the source of these documents and what each document is. After that, we will move on, talk about what happened at the meeting, and we'll talk about where you went and what happened.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Thank you for these documents. This is what I wanted to explain a little earlier on. The first document, the International Committee of the Red Cross dated the 24th of April, 1993, in that document, that document states what I have just said, that in the area of Klisa --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the number is?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: The Court number, D1/367. So looking at this document, I know Ms. Minder I'm informing her, Ms. Minder, of the situation in Konjic, that is to say in Klisa, and I informed her of the fact that many civilians were killed, that many were wounded, and I asked them, because there was no one else to ask, I asked them whether they could help me. And I understand that there is nothing she can do if she's not allowed to do so. So this is a document with which I want to prove that crimes were being perpetrated or rather with which I wanted to draw attention to the fact that crimes were being perpetrated. I had to do this. Furthermore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness's answer just now confirmed the objection I was about to make. I object at this moment until further relevance for all this line of questions is indicated. Again, there has never been a question that crimes were committed by all sides during this terrible war, the Prosecutor should never question that at one moment, and every victim on every side has our full sympathy and our regret for what happened. I mean that quite sincerely. But now we are simply going through a series of meetings about correspondence apparently about this doctor, and I don't question at this moment his good efforts to get medical care to certain locations. Now that may have been a respectable thing to do, Your Honour but how is it relevant to it the issues in this case? Is it a defence against the charges that are charged against Mr. Naletilic? How is this a defence? How is this relevant to the issues in this case? We object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, counsel asked you a question about the source of this document. You just answer that question. As for the contents of this document, we could see by ourselves. And Mr. Krsnik, I think you have to establish the relevancy of this document to this very case. We do not know where you are going to lead us to at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to admit, although I've been a professional for many years it's really necessary to have patience. First of all, the Prosecutor doesn't allow me to -- he should not comment on the Defence's strategy because I didn't comment on his. This is very relevant because this witness is here. This witness has very important information regarding Sovici and Doljani, where the Prosecutor says that my client expelled people, he expelled people from those places and was the overall commander. The witness, and it doesn't matter whether he's a doctor or a priest or an ordinary citizen, on the 5th of April, he was on the site with the highest, with those in the highest positions of the command and he heard and saw the most important matters. I want to prove how this happened. I want to prove this before this Trial Chamber, what happened on the 16th of April in Trusina is not important, neither are the crimes committed against the Croats. That's not important. They don't have to be important at all. But that this witness should explain when he asked for help for one situation they said we have another situation so that we could see how all of this happened, we need to be patient. What the Prosecutor is doing is nothing but obstructing the examination-in-chief. The freedom that a lawyer has to conduct his defence in accordance with the Rules of this Tribunal, when selecting the witness, witnesses, I selected the ones I thought would be able to provide this venerable Trial Chamber with the greatest number of facts and explain the overall situation. If certain things perhaps need to be said, why should there be an objection? Why should an objection be raised immediately, if we want to get what we want to get to, but we can't skip over the fact that there was a meeting in Jablanica and how this happened if we don't hear the entire story. We'll ignore all the Croatian victims it. We will ignore all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: We don't want another war here but may I just say personally if both of you stopped interrupting each other, we could get on much better with the trial. Yesterday, it was Mr. Krsnik interrupting Mr. Scott or Mr. Stringer, and today it's the other way around. I think I understand where this witness is coming from and where you are taking us and it's in relation to persecution. It's rebuttal evidence but let's all just, as Mr. Krsnik said, be patient and Mr. Krsnik, could you try not to get so excited? Now, we are all adults here and let's behave as professionals and if your witness was allowed to tell his story, with interruptions only from us, perhaps we would get there faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think that you are absolutely right. I apologise. Perhaps I wasn't behaving in a professional manner. It came more from the heart perhaps. It's very difficult for me to get used to, to it adapt to the Anglo-Saxon system because I brought in a witness and I thought that he would be allowed to give testimony, and then he starts and he's interrupted. I'm not used to this because the judge has the main word in our system and then the defence and the prosecution present their case once the judges have finished because such objections are not raised in this manner and perhaps I lose my patience in such cases and I apologise for this. This is because I know where the testimony -- where the witness is heading and he is not allowed to do this. He is not allowed to give his testimony. But once more I would like to it apologise, and Your Honour, I think you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you heard all the objections and I would like to ask you to concentrate on the matter and say briefly what these documents represent. Let's turn to the meeting in Jablanica and talk about -- discuss what was -- what issues were addressed at that meeting and then we shall carry on. Please do comment on the documents?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I fear this might not be necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Briefly, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well the document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I wanted to show the chronology of events on the 24th of April, on the 28th of April, and finally the request to Mr. Morales on the 5th of May. That's the chronology. These are documents which I signed. Someone mentioned authenticity. You can find all these documents with the Red Cross, and Mr. Morales from the Spanish Battalion has them too so if they have the same dates and the same signatures then the authenticity cannot be contested. If they don't then that still doesn't mean that I'm lying but I never do lie. So I apologise for this explanation but finally, this meeting was held. So what now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was discussed at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Everything, all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: What was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: All sorts of things. The purpose of the meeting was to visit Croatian places in the Neretva valley where crimes had been committed. That was the first thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 2, the second thing?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, secondly all sorts of matters were discussed there because Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Halilovic finally met face to face and they discussed. And I -- I organised that meeting, it wasn't my -- I do not regret it. They spoke about everything, about the relations between the army and the HVO, and I can remember that Mr. Halilovic persistently told Petkovic, he asked him, "Do we cooperate? Are we cooperating or not?" And then he said, if you're interested in what happened there, he gave the reasons for which the Muslims were brought into a difficult position, why they were expelled, why they had been killed, and I personally asked him, since Morales was there and I think that Marillon arrived later, I asked him who had killed the Muslims up until then and who brought them into such a situation? He never said the Serbs had done it. People might have thought that we did that. And I apologise. Don't regard me just as a doctor. I'm a doctor but I'm also a man. And he said at that point, Halilovic told me, yes, the Serbs did that, but we now have to arrange, we now have to it agree whether we are cooperating with each other or not and we asked us whether we were going to cooperate or not and the crimes had already been committed. So all sorts of matters were discussed at that meeting and I think that there is a recording of that meeting. I think people recorded it. I think perhaps the Spanish Battalion or I don't know who recorded the meeting. And the conclusions of the meeting, the ones that I was most interested were as follows. It was concluded that we would visit these areas in three directions, the areas that I have mentioned. And the condition on which Halilovic agreed to visit these areas where I said that crimes had been committed, and visit them from these three directions, the condition was that he said that we, the HVO, had killed civilians, raped women, in Sovici and Doljani, in these villages and he insisted that we should go there too. And naturally I was in favour of any type of solution. If we could clear things up as we are trying to clear things up now. Mr. Petkovic was the one who would take decisions and he agreed with this too. So we went out into the field and we visited these places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 4th of May, how did you travel and which places did you visit first of all?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well we agreed that we should visit the area from three directions, first of all, number 1, it was the area that the Muslim side had requested, the Doljani and Sovici area. I personally went in that direction. The second direction if I'm not mistaken, was to be this notorious place called Trusina and the area over there. And the third direction, I think it was to be the village of Zabrdje Zaslivlje, or something like that. So there were three different directions. I think that we first of all -- first of all, all of us, I can't be sure, but whether it was just one group that first went to Sovici and Doljani, I'm not sure, or whether we all went there together, I don't know, but what I do know for sure is that Petkovic, Halilovic, and Morales, and myself reached Sovici. We used transport vehicles which belonged to the Spanish Battalion. Together with them, we had an ambulance which accompanied this vehicle. The purpose was to go and to collect any wounded people in the villages, which I asked to go to. I'm waiting for a question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Be so kind, you went there in an armoured personnel carrier. Those are the armoured personnel carriers which belong to the UN which we have seen on video cassettes?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, the standard UN armoured personnel carriers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Jablanica, which village did you reach first of all?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, just a minute. I've got to be very precise here because there might be a misunderstanding. I know both of the villages, I know where they are but at the moment, I don't know which one comes first, Doljani or Sovici, I have no idea but we passed through both villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stop in Doljani and did you speak to the people then, Petkovic, Halilovic, did you visit the houses?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In one of those places, I think it was Doljani, yes, Doljani, we spoke to the civilian population, we spoke to soldiers or rather I can't remember exactly right now. Some were in uniform, some weren't. I'm not sure but I think some of them were but I know that some were detained and I think that was in the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll turn to the school but I'm asking you do you remember when you were in Doljani when you spoke to people there, did you walk around the Doljani - Halilovic, Petkovic, and yourself?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I confused these two villages so we visited both places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you whether in one of the villages, let's put it that way, did you see any houses that had been set on fire? That's the first question, any burnt out houses?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see any burnt houses. And I don't remember any such houses because I was in the armoured personnel carrier among other things. Whether there were burnt houses in those villages or in some hamlets in that area, I really don't know. However, I was in an armoured personnel carrier and -- well, I think this is the most important fact. We went to it a location and the Muslim side had accused the Croats at these locations and they insisted that we should visit them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get out of the armoured personnel carrier then?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you walk around that area?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I can remember the civilians we spoke to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did those civilians say?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: They said that, well as far as I can remember, the main thing that I can remember is that a gentleman from the BH Army were very content, they were very happy. Either they hadn't been civilian victims or there hadn't been any victims but -- well, I don't think there were any civilian victims and whether any of the soldiers had been killed or not, I know. If some of them had been killed, there was a very small number, but they were very happy they were very content because they didn't find what they were afraid of finding and what they had accused of us of. They had accused us of hiding something and when I say us I'm thinking of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember the school in Sovici?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, I should now say we reached the school and we saw detainees in the school, they were detained there. They had been detained by, I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm reluctant to get on my feet after Judge Clark's comments but I am concerned, just for the record, in terms of what the -- where the witness was, said he was a moment ago, I would object to the lack of foundation for particular locations. This was a very mixed area, the evidence, the Chamber will remember from the evidence and going from one hamlet to another hamlet could make a tremendous difference in the thrust of the witness's testimony, where was he in particular -- I asked that we be informed where was he when he had this conversation specifically and if he can identify the person with whom he had this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, you may ask some questions along this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, well, the break is coming up very soon. I'll take all the photographs from Doljani and Sovici and perhaps it will be easier to identify everything then. I didn't think that would be necessary but I see that it is now. So perhaps with the aid of the photographs, the witness might remember things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard the Prosecutor's objection so could you please answer the question?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, we went to both Sovici and Doljani. This I know. We visited civilians in both places. We went to the school. The incriminated school that has been mentioned, in the sense that it has been mentioned. I remember that the soldiers who were detained in that school had many objections to make with regard to their commanders. They objected about how they had been abandoned, betrayed, and so on. I had the impression that they had been promised something but that this promise hadn't been kept. They were very angry with Mr. Halilovic primarily. I think that the most important thing here is the following. Mr. Halilovic and Mr. Pasalic had objections about the relation of the HVO in those two places and maybe with regard to some important event.
